activities.title: Block or point by point?
learnerActions: Compare two model discussion essays on the same question, one organised in blocks and one point by point
Mark where evaluation appears in each
Decide which organisation suits your own question and justify the choice
activities.intendedInsight: Organisation should serve evaluation; point-by-point structures often make it easier to keep evaluating throughout.
activities.rationale: Staging analysis based on Martin and Rose's (2008) description of the discussion genre.

difficulties.pattern: 'A discussion essay should be neutral; I shouldn't give my opinion.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions such as 'there are both advantages and disadvantages'; little or no evaluative language.
difficulties.response: Distinguish fair representation from neutrality and show high-graded discussion essays that reach a qualified judgement. Check the local brief, since a few tasks do ask only for an account of views.

difficulties.pattern: Reported views and the writer's view blur together.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unattributed claims the marker cannot assign to a source or to the writer; apparent shifts of position from paragraph to paragraph.
difficulties.response: Have learners highlight attributed and averred sentences in two colours, then revisit how fair representation of a view differs from endorsing it; teach signal phrases and stance markers that mark the move to the writer's own evaluation (see sta.averral-attribution).

diagnostic.task: Give learners a discussion essay plan and ask them to write its concluding paragraph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Weighs the views and reaches a qualified judgement with reasons and conditions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reaches a judgement that is unrelated to the body or unsupported.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises both sides without any judgement.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: a common entry genre; keep to two perspectives with a short source pack. Pre-sessional: frequently a progression task; emphasise source-based perspectives and early signalling of position. In-sessional undergraduate: link to 'discuss' and 'to what extent' questions in modules and to departmental expectations, which differ in how explicitly a position must be stated.
reviewNotes: EAP materials often treat discussion and argumentative essays as distinct genres; in departmental practice they blur, and the distinction is better taught as a continuum of how early and how strongly the position is stated.

guidance.summary: Comparison is a pervasive rhetorical function in university writing tasks (Moore & Morton, 2005), yet the compare-and-contrast essay is often taught as a symmetrical list of similarities and differences. Teach it instead as comparison in the service of a point: criteria are chosen because they matter to the question, and the essay says what the comparison reveals. Carrell (1985) found that explicitly teaching top-level text structures, comparison among them, helped L2 readers; the same structural awareness can be developed for writing by analysing exemplars before production.

activities.title: Criteria first
learnerActions: Given two items and a question, brainstorm possible points of comparison
Select the three most relevant to the question and justify the selection
Build a comparison grid and decide what the overall pattern shows
Write a thesis statement that states the outcome of the comparison
activities.intendedInsight: Criteria are chosen for relevance to the question, and the thesis states what the comparison shows.
activities.rationale: Shifts the task from description to purpose-driven comparison, reflecting the evaluative emphasis of university writing tasks (Moore & Morton, 2005).

activities.title: Restructure the blocks
learnerActions: Read a block-organised draft that describes item A and then item B
Highlight each criterion in a different colour across both blocks
Rewrite one section point by point with explicit comparative language
Discuss which version makes the significance of the differences clearer
activities.intendedInsight: Point-by-point organisation tends to make comparison explicit; block organisation needs deliberate cross-referencing.
activities.rationale: Develops awareness of comparison as a text structure (Carrell, 1985) and transfers it to production.

difficulties.pattern: 'Compare means describe A, then describe B.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Two descriptive halves with comparison appearing only in the conclusion.
difficulties.response: Require a cross-referencing sentence in each paragraph and teach point-by-point organisation first. Do not forbid block organisation: it is acceptable when each block makes the comparison explicit.

difficulties.pattern: Listing similarities and differences without saying why they matter.
difficulties.revealedBy: No thesis, or a conclusion that restates the list.
difficulties.response: After each paragraph ask what the difference means for the question, and model evaluative sentences that answer it.

diagnostic.task: Ask learners to state in two sentences the outcome of comparing two familiar options (for example two ways of revising for exams) on criteria they choose.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names relevant criteria and states an outcome tied to them.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Lists differences without stating an outcome.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes each option separately.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: a manageable early genre that builds comparative language; use familiar items. Pre-sessional: move to comparing theories, models or policies using sources. In-sessional undergraduate: comparison questions occur across disciplines (theoretical approaches, cases, texts, methods), where the criteria themselves are disciplinary and should come from the module.
reviewNotes: There is little genre-analytic research on the compare-and-contrast essay as a distinct student genre; this guidance draws on research on comparison as a rhetorical function and as a text structure.

guidance.summary: Martin and Rose (2008) distinguish sequential, factorial and consequential explanations, giving learners a principled choice of structure depending on whether a question asks how something happens, why it happens or what it leads to. Gardner and Nesi (2013) identify Explanation as a distinct genre family in university assessment whose purpose is demonstrating knowledge and understanding. Halliday and Martin (1993) show how scientific explanation packages causal reasoning into nominal groups and verbs such as lead to, which is both a resource and a source of difficulty. The central teaching challenge is moving from naming causes to explaining mechanisms and calibrating certainty.

activities.title: Cause, consequence or mechanism?
learnerActions: Sort six essay and exam questions by whether they ask for causes, consequences or a sequence
Choose an organising pattern for each (factorial, consequential, sequential)
Plan one essay, ranking factors by importance and giving a reason for the ranking
activities.intendedInsight: The question determines the type of explanation and therefore the essay's structure.
activities.rationale: Applies Martin and Rose's (2008) explanation types as planning choices.

activities.title: From naming to explaining
learnerActions: Read a paragraph that lists three causes in one sentence each
For one cause, add the mechanism (how it produces the effect) and supporting evidence
Adjust the strength of the causal verb and add hedging where the evidence is correlational
Compare your paragraph with a model
activities.intendedInsight: Explanation requires a mechanism and calibrated certainty, not a list of factors.
activities.rationale: Targets the step from listing to explaining; Halliday and Martin (1993) show how causal relations are realised in scientific explanation, giving learners language to model.

difficulties.pattern: Listing causes without explaining how they operate.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs of one claim plus one example; repeated 'Another reason is ...'.
difficulties.response: Prompt with 'How exactly does this lead to ...?' and model mechanism sentences. Do not respond by supplying more connectors: the gap is explanatory content, not linking.

difficulties.pattern: Overstating causation ('X causes Y') on the basis of correlational evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unhedged causal verbs attached to survey or correlational findings.
difficulties.response: Review correlation and causation using examples from the learners' own sources, then practise rewording with 'is associated with' or 'may contribute to'.

difficulties.pattern: Causal connectors used interchangeably regardless of the structure that follows (for example 'due to the population increased').
difficulties.revealedBy: Prepositional causal expressions followed by clauses, or conjunctions followed by noun phrases.
difficulties.response: Where a learner's other languages use one causal connective before both clauses and noun phrases, contrast prepositional patterns (because of, due to + noun phrase) with conjunctive ones (because, since + clause), and practise nominalising the cause.

diagnostic.task: Give learners a simple causal diagram and ask for a three-sentence explanation of it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains the mechanism with accurate causal language and appropriate hedging.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Uses accurate causal language but gives no mechanism.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists the elements linked by 'and' or 'also'.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: explanations of familiar processes and causes, often linked to subject-content modules, form a strong bridge into science and social science. Pre-sessional: source-based explanation with hedged causal claims. In-sessional undergraduate: explanation essays and exam answers in the sciences, social sciences and humanities (for example historical causation), where disciplinary norms for causal argument differ.

guidance.summary: Hoey's (1983, 2001) situation–problem–response–evaluation pattern is the backbone of this genre and shows learners that a response is only complete once it is evaluated; a negative evaluation recycles the pattern towards a new response. Swales and Feak (2012) treat problem–process–solution texts as a foundational academic pattern. Teach the genre as evaluative, since the commonest weakness is presenting solutions without criteria, and use it as a bridge to case studies, business reports and policy briefs.

activities.title: Mapping the pattern
learnerActions: Read a short problem–solution text and label the situation, problem, response and evaluation
Identify the signalling nouns that mark each element
Find a place where a negative evaluation leads to a new response
Plan your own essay as a chain of these elements
activities.intendedInsight: The pattern is recursive, and evaluation is what makes it analytical.
activities.rationale: Hoey's pattern gives learners a functional map with recognisable lexical signals (Hoey, 1983, 2001).

activities.title: Criteria matrix for solutions
learnerActions: List possible responses to a problem from a source pack
Agree four criteria such as effectiveness, cost, feasibility and unintended consequences
Rate each response against the criteria with evidence
Write a recommendation paragraph that justifies the choice and acknowledges trade-offs
activities.intendedInsight: Recommendations persuade when they are justified by explicit criteria and honest about trade-offs.
activities.rationale: Turns the evaluation element of the pattern into an explicit, criterion-based procedure that learners can reuse in report and case-study genres.

difficulties.pattern: Describing the problem at length and listing solutions in a final paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Most of the word count spent on background; solutions named but not evaluated.
difficulties.response: Set word budgets for each stage and require an evaluation for every response proposed.

difficulties.pattern: Recommendations phrased as unconditional commands ('The government must ban ...').
difficulties.revealedBy: Strong 'must' and 'should' statements without justification or attention to feasibility, often carried over from test-essay practice.
difficulties.response: Contrast hortatory statements with justified, hedged recommendations and teach alternatives such as 'a more feasible option would be ...'.

diagnostic.task: Ask learners to identify the problem, response and evaluation in a 150-word text and say whether the evaluation is positive or negative.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Labels every element and points to the signals that mark them.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds the problem and response but misses or misreads the evaluation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the text without identifying the pattern.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: familiar problems with short source packs, closely linked to recommending language. Pre-sessional: source-based evaluation of responses, often a progression essay type. In-sessional undergraduate: common in social sciences, environmental studies, engineering and health, and a natural step towards case-study and report genres.

guidance.summary: Exam essays are a high-stakes genre that is largely absent from corpora of assessed coursework, so teaching should be built on local past papers, examiners' comments and departmental guidance. Horowitz's (1986) analysis of essay examination prompts (proposed reference) suggests that exam questions typically ask writers to select and organise known content in response to specific demands, which makes question analysis and selective use of revised material central. Weigle (2002) discusses how timed, impromptu writing constrains planning and revision; practice should therefore build fast planning routines, not only language. Make clear that university exam essays differ from proficiency-test essays: they are judged mainly on disciplinary content and its use, not on language display.

activities.title: Five-minute plans
learnerActions: Read three past-paper questions
For each, spend five minutes writing only a thesis and a three-point plan
Swap plans and judge whether each point answers the question as set
Choose one plan and write its introduction in eight minutes
activities.intendedInsight: Many marks are won or lost in planning and relevance rather than in language.
activities.rationale: Builds the fast planning routines that timed conditions constrain (Weigle, 2002).

activities.title: Revise for questions, not topics
learnerActions: Take a set of revision notes on one topic
Write four different exam questions that could be set on that topic
For each question, mark which notes are relevant and which are not
Write one paragraph for one question using only relevant notes
activities.intendedInsight: Selecting and reorganising content for the question is the core exam-essay skill; reproducing everything learned is not.
activities.rationale: Responds to the content-selection demands identified in analyses of essay examination prompts (Horowitz, 1986, proposed).

difficulties.pattern: 'I will write down everything I memorised about the topic.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Long descriptive answers loosely related to the question; a prepared essay adapted awkwardly to a different question.
difficulties.response: Practise answering differently worded questions on the same topic, spending the first minutes on question analysis and a plan, and mark for relevance first. Avoid encouraging memorised model essays as the main revision strategy.

difficulties.pattern: Running out of time and leaving answers unfinished.
difficulties.revealedBy: A long first answer and incomplete final answers.
difficulties.response: Practise time allocation under realistic conditions and teach a fallback of bullet-point conclusions when time runs out. Do not focus only on shortening introductions; uneven allocation and skipped planning are usually the cause.

difficulties.pattern: Anxiety leading to blanking or loss of planned structure.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report blanking; answers that start well and then lose direction.
difficulties.response: Rehearse a plan-first routine under realistic conditions so that it becomes automatic, and signpost anxiety-management strategies and support services.

diagnostic.task: Give a past-paper question and ask the learner to write only the plan and introduction in ten minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The introduction answers the question directly and the plan's points are relevant and logically ordered.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The plan is relevant but the introduction is generic or defers the answer.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A topic-focused plan that does not address the question's demand.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: many foundation programmes assess subject content through exams, so focus on question analysis and timed planning. Pre-sessional: timed writing appears in some progression assessments but differs from disciplinary exams; make the distinction explicit. In-sessional undergraduate: subject-specific practice with past papers, ideally with subject staff. Taught postgraduate: exams are less frequent but often require application to cases, and some programmes use seen or open-book formats.
reviewNotes: Part of the summary rests on a proposed reference (Horowitz, 1986, on essay examination prompts); if it cannot be verified, remove that sentence and the related activity rationale.
Corpora of proficient student writing such as BAWE consist mainly of coursework, so genre-analytic evidence on exam essays is thin.

guidance.summary: Short answers serve the purpose of demonstrating knowledge and understanding that Gardner and Nesi (2013) associate with the Exercise and Explanation genre families. The main transfer problem is essay habits (introductions, restating the question, elaboration) that cost time and earn no marks. Teach command words and mark allocation, model formal definitions of the term–class–distinguishing-feature type described in rhetorical analyses of scientific English (Trimble, 1985), and use subject-specific past papers, because what counts as a complete answer is disciplinary.

activities.title: Marks to points
learnerActions: Read short-answer questions with their mark allocations
Predict how many distinct points each requires
Compare your predictions with a marking scheme or teacher model
Rewrite a padded answer so that it fits the marks available
activities.intendedInsight: Mark allocation signals expected content; length should follow content, not effort.
activities.rationale: Makes the economy of knowledge-display genres explicit (Gardner & Nesi, 2013).

activities.title: Definition upgrade
learnerActions: Read a set of informal definitions ('Osmosis is when water moves')
Rewrite each as term + class + distinguishing features
Add an example only where it would earn credit
Check accuracy against a subject glossary with a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Formal definitions are compact and precise, and are often exactly what the marks are for.
activities.rationale: Uses the definitional pattern described in rhetorical analyses of scientific and technical English (Trimble, 1985).

difficulties.pattern: Writing a mini-essay with an introduction and conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Restated questions, background sentences and time overruns on short items.
difficulties.response: Show marking schemes and practise first-sentence answers. Do not present this as 'style does not matter': accuracy and terminology still carry the marks.

difficulties.pattern: Identifying without explaining in 'explain' questions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that name a factor but give no reason or mechanism.
difficulties.response: Contrast 'state' and 'explain' answers to the same item and teach extensions such as 'because ...' and 'which means that ...'.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to answer 'Define X and explain why it matters (4 marks)' on a familiar topic.
diagnostic.strongResponse: An accurate formal definition and two developed points, with no padding.
diagnostic.partialResponse: An accurate definition with an undeveloped explanation, or a padded answer.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A vague or circular definition.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: highly relevant because subject modules often use short-answer tests; link closely to content teaching. In-sessional undergraduate: support for first-year science, health and social science assessments, ideally agreeing with subject tutors what counts as a full answer.
reviewNotes: There is little EAP genre research on short-answer responses as such; this guidance extrapolates from work on definitions and on knowledge-display genres.

guidance.summary: Gardner and Nesi (2013) place the Critique family among genres whose purpose is developing independent reasoning, and Swales and Feak (2012) treat critiques as a core graduate writing task in which evaluation must be grounded and appropriately mitigated. Wallace and Wray (2016) offer critical questions about a text's claims, evidence and contribution that learners can turn into explicit evaluation criteria. Teach the balance between summary and evaluation explicitly, because briefs vary (some want very little summary), and check the local brief for required criteria or headings.

activities.title: Criteria before reading
learnerActions: Before reading, agree evaluation criteria suited to the text type (empirical, review or theoretical)
Read and note evidence for each criterion with page references
Classify each note as a strength or limitation, and as minor or major
Write one judgement sentence that weighs the major points
activities.intendedInsight: Critique is criterion-based judgement, not personal agreement.
activities.rationale: Operationalises the critical-questions approach of Wallace and Wray (2016).

activities.title: Mitigating criticism
learnerActions: Read a set of blunt evaluative sentences ('The study is useless because the sample is small')
Rewrite them using hedging, praise–criticism pairs and specific consequences for the claims
Compare your versions with evaluative sentences in published reviews
activities.intendedInsight: Academic critique is specific, reasoned and courteous, and mitigation adds to rather than weakens the critic's credibility.
activities.rationale: Swales and Feak (2012) address evaluative language in critiques, and Hyland's (2004) analysis of reviews shows how academic critics typically temper criticism.

difficulties.pattern: 'Being critical means finding faults.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reviews that list only weaknesses, often in a dismissive tone.
difficulties.response: Show that evaluation weighs strengths and limitations relative to the text's purpose, and require at least one justified strength.

difficulties.pattern: Reluctance to criticise published experts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summary-only reviews, or evaluation limited to praise.
difficulties.response: Frame critique as a disciplinary expectation and a form of respectful engagement, and model criterion-based, mitigated criticism. Avoid attributing the reluctance to a national 'culture'; it usually reflects prior assessment expectations.

difficulties.pattern: Summary takes up most of the word count.
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluation confined to a final short paragraph.
difficulties.response: Set word budgets from the brief and practise 100-word summaries of the same article.

diagnostic.task: Give learners a 150-word critique paragraph and ask them to identify its criterion, its evidence and its judgement.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies all three and comments on whether the evidence justifies the judgement.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the judgement but not the criterion or evidence.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats the paragraph as a summary.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional: often the first source-evaluation genre; use accessible articles and shared criteria. In-sessional undergraduate: article critiques are common in psychology, health, education and the social sciences, and criteria are disciplinary (for example validity in psychology). Taught postgraduate: critiques of empirical studies prepare for literature reviews and dissertation methodology, and expectations of methodological critique rise.

guidance.summary: Hyland's (2004) study of published book reviews shows that reviewers commonly temper criticism, for example by pairing it with praise or hedging it, and that evaluative practices differ across disciplines. Swales and Feak (2012) treat reviews as a form of critique with particular audience demands. For student assignments, clarify whether the task is a disciplinary book review or a book-length critique; for doctoral researchers a published book review is a common first publication and an introduction to their field's review practices, so analysing recent reviews in a target journal is the best preparation.

activities.title: Anatomy of a review
learnerActions: Read two reviews from a journal in your field
Label the stages: bibliographic details, context, description, evaluation, recommendation
Highlight praise in one colour and criticism in another, and note how criticism is softened
Write a short style sheet for reviews in that journal
activities.intendedInsight: Reviews have recognisable stages and evaluative conventions that vary by venue and discipline.
activities.rationale: Learner-led analysis that tests Hyland's (2004) observations about praise and criticism in learners' own fields.

activities.title: Writing for readers
learnerActions: Identify two possible readerships for a book (for example specialists and new postgraduates)
Write a short recommendation for each
Discuss how evaluation and terminology change between the two
activities.intendedInsight: Reviews are written for readers deciding whether to read; evaluation is tied to readership.
activities.rationale: Applies the audience orientation that Swales and Feak (2012) emphasise in evaluative genres.

difficulties.pattern: Chapter-by-chapter summary with a brief evaluation at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Description dominates and evaluation is confined to the last paragraph.
difficulties.response: Require evaluative comment within descriptive sections and set a word budget for description.

difficulties.pattern: A tone that is either harsh or wholly deferential.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unmitigated criticism, or unreserved praise with no limitations noted.
difficulties.response: Compare hedged and unhedged versions of the same evaluation and analyse how published reviewers in the field calibrate theirs.

diagnostic.task: Ask learners to write two sentences evaluating a book they know, one on a strength and one on a limitation, for a stated reader.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Specific, mitigated and oriented to the stated reader.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Specific but unmitigated, or mitigated but vague.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Expresses personal liking or disliking.

guidance.contextNotes: In-sessional undergraduate: book reviews occur mainly in the humanities and some social sciences, often as a first exercise in a published evaluative genre. Taught postgraduate: reviews of key texts on programme reading lists. PGR: published book reviews are a common early publication, and venue conventions and editors' expectations are the priority.
reviewNotes: Tagged EGAP because its features are shared across fields, but book reviews are concentrated in the humanities and social sciences and rare in science and engineering coursework; designers may treat it as ESAP for those programmes.

guidance.summary: Reflective writing draws on Schön's (1983) account of the reflective practitioner and is commonly scaffolded with models such as Gibbs's (1988) reflective cycle. Moon (2004) distinguishes descriptive writing from progressively deeper levels of reflection, which helps make markers' expectations explicit. Ryan (2011) argues that reflective writing must be taught as an academic genre with specific linguistic resources, for example the shift from past-tense reporting to present-tense reasoning and future-oriented reconstruction, rather than assumed to come naturally. Because reflective conventions range from personal journals to formal assignments with citations, the brief and local exemplars must guide the form.

activities.title: Depth ladder
learnerActions: Read four extracts reflecting on the same incident at different depths
Rank them and agree what distinguishes each level
Highlight language that signals analysis ('this may have been because', 'in light of')
Rewrite a descriptive extract so that it reaches the next level
activities.intendedInsight: Depth comes from interpretation, questioning and links to theory, not from more detail or stronger emotion.
activities.rationale: Based on Moon's (2004) distinction between descriptive writing and deeper levels of reflection; it makes tacit criteria visible.

activities.title: Mapping reflective language by stage
learnerActions: Analyse a model reflection and label its reporting and responding, relating, reasoning and reconstructing stages
Note tense, pronoun and modal choices in each stage
Draft your own reflection stage by stage with a language bank
Peer-check that each stage does its job
activities.intendedInsight: Each reflective stage has typical language; reflection is a learnable academic genre.
activities.rationale: Applies Ryan's (2011) social semiotic account of reflective writing and the 4Rs scaffold she adapted from earlier work by Bain and colleagues.

difficulties.pattern: 'Reflection is just describing what happened and how I felt.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Narrative-dominated texts with little analysis; feelings reported without interpretation.
difficulties.response: Use word budgets per stage and the depth ladder. Do not respond by discouraging feelings altogether: feelings are data to be analysed.

difficulties.pattern: Discomfort with the first person and with personal disclosure in assessed writing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Impersonal reflections that avoid 'I', or, conversely, disclosure beyond what the task needs.
difficulties.response: Explain that the first person is expected here and that 'never use I' is not a rule of academic writing; discuss what to disclose, and how to protect privacy and confidentiality.

difficulties.pattern: Mechanical use of a reflective cycle as a set of headings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Six headings with one short paragraph each and a superficial action plan.
difficulties.response: Present models as thinking tools, compare formulaic and integrated reflections, and check the brief on whether headings are expected.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to spend ten minutes reflecting in writing on a recent learning experience in the course.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Brief description, analysis with reasons, a link to a concept or source, and a specific future action.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some analysis but no link to theory, or a vague action ('I will work harder').
diagnostic.gapResponse: Narrative and feelings only.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: reflective learning logs and reflections on progress build the genre's language. In-sessional undergraduate: reflective assignments in education, nursing, business and engineering placements, where models and criteria differ. Taught postgraduate: reflective components of professional master's programmes usually require explicit links to theory; see also the professional practice portfolio.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with dhl.reflective-practice (health-specific) and lrn.reflective-logs; this topic covers the general assessed genre.

guidance.summary: Horowitz (1986) found annotated bibliographies among the writing tasks university teachers actually set, and Gardner and Nesi (2013) place them in the Literature Survey family, whose purpose is building research skills. The genre is a useful scaffold because it isolates three skills (summarising, evaluating and judging relevance) that literature reviews later integrate. Briefs vary considerably (descriptive or evaluative annotations, word limits, ordering), so analyse the local brief first. Johns and Mayes (1990) found that less proficient summarisers relied more heavily on copying from the source, a risk that is acute when annotations are written from abstracts.

activities.title: Three-layer annotation
learnerActions: Read an article and write one sentence on its purpose and approach and two on its findings
Add one or two evaluative sentences that use explicit criteria
Add one sentence on relevance to your project
Colour-code the three layers and check that the evaluation is not disguised description
activities.intendedInsight: Annotations combine summary, evaluation and relevance, each with its own language.
activities.rationale: Separating the layers mirrors the main variations in annotated-bibliography briefs and prepares for later synthesis in literature reviews (Gardner & Nesi, 2013).

activities.title: An abstract is not an annotation
learnerActions: Compare a source's abstract with a model annotation of the same source
Identify what the annotation adds and what it leaves out
Rewrite an annotation that was copied from an abstract
activities.intendedInsight: Annotations are written for a different purpose and reader from an abstract.
activities.rationale: Targets the reliance on source wording that Johns and Mayes (1990) observed in less proficient summary writers.

difficulties.pattern: Annotations that paraphrase the abstract.
difficulties.revealedBy: Close textual similarity to abstracts; no evaluation or relevance comment.
difficulties.response: Ask for annotations written from notes on the full text, and show that evaluation and relevance require the writer's own judgement.

difficulties.pattern: Evaluation based on surface features ('a good article because it is recent and long').
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic evaluative comments that could apply to any source.
difficulties.response: Provide evaluation criteria tied to source type, such as sample and design for empirical studies or scope and currency for reviews.

diagnostic.task: Give learners an annotation containing summary, evaluation and relevance sentences and ask them to label each sentence's function.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Labels every sentence correctly and comments on the adequacy of the evaluation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the summary but confuses evaluation with relevance.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot distinguish summary from evaluation.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: annotated bibliographies scaffold extended projects. In-sessional undergraduate: often a preparatory assessment before a dissertation or major essay. Taught postgraduate: used as a staged assessment before literature reviews, with higher expectations of evaluation.

guidance.summary: Feak and Swales (2009) present the literature review as telling a research story, with attention to organisation, citation choices and the writer's stance towards the literature. Wallace and Wray (2016) provide a framework for critical engagement with literature that makes evaluation explicit. Coursework literature reviews belong to Gardner and Nesi's (2013) Literature Survey family, whose purpose is building research skills; they differ from review sections in research articles and theses (res.literature-review) because the gap often serves a coursework question rather than justifying the writer's own study. Emphasise synthesis over serial summary, and analyse local exemplars, because expectations range from narrative reviews to systematic-style reviews with documented searches.

activities.title: From list to synthesis
learnerActions: Read a source-by-source review extract
Use a synthesis matrix to regroup its sources by theme
Rewrite one paragraph led by a thematic topic sentence in your own voice, with sources in dialogue
Compare the two versions for voice and evaluation
activities.intendedInsight: Reviews are organised by ideas, and sources serve the writer's points.
activities.rationale: Targets the serial-summary pattern and the questions of organisation and stance discussed by Feak and Swales (2009).

activities.title: Critical questions for the review
learnerActions: For your review question, list what is known, how it is known and what is disputed
Apply critical questions about claims, evidence and warrants to three key sources
Write a paragraph that evaluates the evidence base for one theme
activities.intendedInsight: A literature review evaluates the evidence base rather than simply reporting it.
activities.rationale: Uses Wallace and Wray's (2016) critical reading framework as a writing scaffold.

difficulties.pattern: Source-by-source summaries ('Smith (2019) found ... Jones (2020) argued ...').
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs beginning with author names; few comparative or evaluative statements.
difficulties.response: Require thematic topic sentences in the writer's voice and use synthesis matrices. Do not ban integral citation; teach when author prominence is rhetorically useful.

difficulties.pattern: Unsupported or absolute gap claims ('no research has been done on this').
difficulties.revealedBy: Unhedged gap statements, or gaps unrelated to the literature reviewed.
difficulties.response: Teach hedged gap language and require that every gap claim follows from the reviewed literature.

difficulties.pattern: Uncertainty about what to include and how much is enough.
difficulties.revealedBy: Over-inclusive reviews that cover everything found; anxiety about missing sources.
difficulties.response: Agree scope criteria tied to the question and keep a search record; explain that coverage depends on the review's purpose.

diagnostic.task: Show two paragraphs reviewing the same three sources, one serial and one synthesised, and ask which is stronger and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Prefers the synthesised paragraph and explains its use of voice, comparison and evaluation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Prefers the synthesised paragraph but cannot say why.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Prefers the serial version as clearer.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional: short literature reviews within extended projects, often with provided sources. In-sessional undergraduate: reviews in second and final years, frequently preparing for dissertations. Taught postgraduate: stand-alone reviews and dissertation review chapters, with rising expectations of critical evaluation and justified scope.

guidance.summary: Horowitz (1986) found summary of, and reaction to, reading among the tasks university teachers set, and Hirvela (2004) argues that connecting reading and writing, with summary and response at its centre, is fundamental to L2 writing instruction. Leki and Carson (1997) contrasted EAP writing that could draw on personal knowledge with content-course writing that held students responsible for source texts; summary–response builds that text-responsible stance. Grabe and Zhang (2013) argue that reading and writing should be taught together, with explicit attention to summarising and responding.

activities.title: Two-colour paper
learnerActions: Read a model summary–response
Highlight summary sentences in one colour and response sentences in another
Note the signal phrases and reporting verbs at the boundary
Find any sentence that mixes the two and rewrite it
activities.intendedInsight: Readers need to know whose idea is whose, and the boundary is marked linguistically.
activities.rationale: Makes visible the text-responsible stance described by Leki and Carson (1997).

activities.title: Respond to a claim, not a topic
learnerActions: Identify the source's three main claims
Choose one and draft agree, disagree and qualify responses, each with a reason
Select the strongest and develop it with evidence
activities.intendedInsight: A response must engage the source's argument rather than the general topic.
activities.rationale: Applies the reading–writing integration Hirvela (2004) advocates.

difficulties.pattern: Evaluation leaking into the summary ('The author wrongly claims ...').
difficulties.revealedBy: Loaded reporting verbs and evaluative adjectives in the summary section.
difficulties.response: Contrast neutral and evaluative reporting verbs and reserve evaluation for the response.

difficulties.pattern: The response addresses the general topic rather than the text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Opinion essays only loosely connected to the source's argument.
difficulties.response: Require the response to quote or paraphrase the specific claim it answers.

diagnostic.task: Ask learners to write a three-sentence summary and a two-sentence response to a short argumentative paragraph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: An accurate, attributed summary and a response that engages a specific claim with a reason.
diagnostic.partialResponse: An accurate summary followed by a generic response.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Copies the source, or gives an opinion without a summary.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: a key entry genre into source-based writing. Pre-sessional: frequent in early weeks and closely related to integrated reading-into-writing tasks. In-sessional undergraduate: appears as reading responses and seminar papers, particularly in the humanities and social sciences.
reviewNotes: The summary–response paper is mainly a North American composition genre; in UK contexts it is more often an EAP or foundation teaching genre than a departmental assessment.

guidance.summary: Nesi and Gardner (2012) show that 'report' is a label applied to several distinct genre families (methodology recounts, research reports, design specifications and case studies among them), so report conventions should be taught as a family resemblance rather than a single template. Gardner and Nesi's (2013) classification helps learners locate the report they have been set. Bruce's (2008) distinction between social genres and the cognitive genres within them shows learners that a report may contain explanation, discussion or recount. Contrast essay and report on the same content, emphasise the reader who reads selectively and acts on findings, and always check the brief and templates.

activities.title: Essay to report
learnerActions: Read a short essay and the brief for a report on the same topic
Identify the report's reader and what decision or understanding they need
Restructure the essay into headed sections
Write informative headings and decide where a table would serve better than prose
activities.intendedInsight: Report structure serves a reader who reads selectively and needs findings and recommendations.
activities.rationale: Holding content constant while changing the genre isolates purpose and reader, the factors that distinguish the report families described by Nesi and Gardner (2012).

activities.title: Which report is this?
learnerActions: Examine extracts from a lab report, a business report and a design report
Compare their sections, headings and use of visuals
Agree which features are shared and which are specific to each
activities.intendedInsight: 'Report' covers several genres, and the shared features are fewer than learners expect.
activities.rationale: Based on Gardner and Nesi's (2013) classification of genre families in student writing.

difficulties.pattern: 'A report is an essay with headings.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Headings inserted into continuous argumentative prose; no separation of findings from recommendations.
difficulties.response: Show reports in which sections do different jobs and ask what the reader of each section needs. Do not imply that reports contain no argument: analysis and justification remain central.

difficulties.pattern: Uninformative or generic headings ('Part 1', 'Main body').
difficulties.revealedBy: Headings that do not tell the reader what a section contains.
difficulties.response: Practise writing headings a reader could navigate by, and check them against the template.

difficulties.pattern: Visuals inserted without number, caption or reference in the text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Figures that the text never mentions or explains.
difficulties.response: Teach captioning and in-text reference together, and require every visual to be cited and commented on.

diagnostic.task: Ask: what are three differences between an essay and a report?
diagnostic.strongResponse: Mentions purpose and reader, selective reading supported by headings, separation of findings from conclusions or recommendations, and integrated visuals.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions headings only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot name a difference.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: introduce through simple reports in subject modules. Pre-sessional: often the format of the progression project. In-sessional undergraduate: reports in science, engineering, business and social science differ substantially, so work from departmental templates. Taught postgraduate: professional report formats and dissertation-style reports.

guidance.summary: Parkinson (2017) characterises the student laboratory report as a genre in its own right that differs from the research article it superficially resembles, notably because it is written to demonstrate understanding of established theory and procedure rather than to claim a new contribution. Gardner and Nesi (2013) classify lab reports with Methodology Recounts. Teach section by section with the department's lab manual, attending to data commentary (Swales & Feak, 2012) and to the discussion of error, which students frequently reduce to generic statements. Conventions such as passive or active voice, and whether results and discussion are combined, vary by discipline and lab manual and should be checked locally.

activities.title: Results or discussion?
learnerActions: Sort sentences from a lab report into results (what was found) and discussion (what it means)
Identify the language that distinguishes them, such as tense, hedging and comparison with theory
Rewrite a mixed paragraph as separate results and discussion paragraphs
activities.intendedInsight: Results report and highlight; discussion interprets and evaluates.
activities.rationale: Builds awareness of section functions as described in genre analysis of student lab reports (Parkinson, 2017).

activities.title: Beyond 'human error'
learnerActions: List possible sources of error in a familiar experiment
Classify them as systematic or random, procedural or instrumental
Estimate the direction and approximate size of each one's effect on the result
Write an evaluation paragraph that ends with a specific improvement
activities.intendedInsight: Error analysis is reasoning about specific effects on results, not a ritual admission of imperfection.
activities.rationale: Makes explicit the evaluative expectations of the discussion section, which generic error statements do not meet; the activity draws on data commentary principles (Swales & Feak, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: Method written as instructions copied from the lab manual ('Add 5 ml of ...').
difficulties.revealedBy: Imperative sentences in the method section.
difficulties.response: Contrast manual instructions with a report method and practise converting them to past-tense description, passive or active according to the local convention. Do not teach that the passive is always required.

difficulties.pattern: Results described vaguely, without values or figure references, or mixed with interpretation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Statements such as 'the graph goes up' and explanations embedded in the results.
difficulties.response: Teach location and highlighting statements that cite values and figure numbers, and move interpretation to the discussion.

difficulties.pattern: Introduction written as a general history of the topic or as a research-gap argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long background with no link between theory and the aim of the experiment.
difficulties.response: Analyse departmental exemplar introductions and focus on the theory needed to interpret this experiment.

diagnostic.task: Give learners a short results table and ask for two sentences of results and two of discussion.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Results sentences cite values and the table; discussion sentences interpret them against theory.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Cites values but mixes interpretation into the results.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the whole table without selecting what matters.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: science foundation students write lab reports early, usually with structured templates. In-sessional undergraduate: discipline-specific support, ideally embedded with lab staff, since conventions differ between chemistry, physics, biology and engineering. Taught postgraduate: lab-based MSc students may need support in moving towards research-article conventions for project reports.
reviewNotes: Claims about Parkinson (2017) are stated at a general level; reviewers should check the article's specific move findings before adding detail.

guidance.summary: Nesi and Gardner (2012) identify the Research Report as a genre family in which students report their own investigations, usually later in a programme. Swales and Feak (2012) give accessible, move-based treatments of research-reporting sections, and Creswell and Creswell (2018) offer frameworks for aligning questions, design and reporting across quantitative, qualitative and mixed approaches. Emphasise alignment between questions, methods, findings and conclusions, and proportionate claims from small samples. On pre-sessionals the project is also a vehicle for academic socialisation, so keep its scope modest and its process visible.

activities.title: Alignment audit
learnerActions: Write your research questions at the top of a page
For each question, note the method, data and finding that address it
Mark any finding not linked to a question and any question without a finding
Revise the questions or the conclusions to restore alignment
activities.intendedInsight: Coherence in a report comes from alignment between questions, methods, findings and conclusions.
activities.rationale: Applies the design alignment emphasised by Creswell and Creswell (2018) to the student's own report.

activities.title: Claims sized to data
learnerActions: Read conclusions from three student projects
Rate the strength of each claim against the sample size and design
Rewrite overclaims with hedges and explicit scope limits
activities.intendedInsight: Small-scale studies support modest, bounded claims, and stating limits strengthens credibility.
activities.rationale: Builds claim calibration in the context where learners most often overclaim: reporting their own first research.

difficulties.pattern: Generalising from small samples ('This proves that students prefer ...').
difficulties.revealedBy: Unhedged generalisations beyond the participants studied.
difficulties.response: Teach scope language and the limitations section together. Do not discourage claims altogether; the aim is claims that the data can bear.

difficulties.pattern: Literature review and discussion disconnected from each other.
difficulties.revealedBy: A discussion that never returns to the sources reviewed.
difficulties.response: Require each discussion paragraph to relate a finding to at least one reviewed source.

difficulties.pattern: Research questions too broad to answer with the data available.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions such as 'What is the impact of social media on society?'
difficulties.response: Narrow by population, context and variable or phenomenon, and check feasibility before data collection.

diagnostic.task: Give learners a research question and ask what data could answer it and what claims would then be possible.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Proposes feasible data and states bounded claims.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Proposes feasible data but overclaims.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Proposes unfeasible or misaligned data.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional: extended projects of modest scope, often using secondary data or small primary datasets, where process and alignment matter more than results. In-sessional undergraduate: research methods modules and final-year projects, with disciplinary conventions for quantitative and qualitative reporting. Taught postgraduate: projects that prepare for or form part of the dissertation.

guidance.summary: Gardner and Nesi (2013) classify case studies among genres that prepare students for professional practice, and Horowitz (1986) found case studies among the tasks university teachers set. Nathan's (2013) analysis of the business case report describes a problem-oriented genre organised around analysis and recommendations and distinct from the essay. The central challenge is analytical application: frameworks and theories must be used to explain the case, not summarised. Because the genre varies so much across fields (a nursing case study differs markedly from a business case report), analyse departmental exemplars and briefs.

activities.title: Facts, inferences, assumptions
learnerActions: Read a short case and list its facts
List the inferences you draw and the evidence for each
Identify assumptions that would need checking
Write a short statement of the main issue grounded in the facts
activities.intendedInsight: Analysis rests on distinguishing what the case states from what the analyst infers.
activities.rationale: Supports the analytical stance expected in professional-practice genres (Gardner & Nesi, 2013).

activities.title: Framework as lens, not list
learnerActions: Compare two paragraphs applying the same framework to a case, one descriptive and one analytical
Identify how the analytical paragraph uses case evidence and draws implications
Rewrite a descriptive paragraph analytically
activities.intendedInsight: Frameworks earn credit when they reveal something about the case.
activities.rationale: Reflects the analysis-and-recommendation focus Nathan (2013) describes in business case reports.

difficulties.pattern: Retelling the case.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long summaries of the case at the expense of analysis.
difficulties.response: Tell learners to assume the marker knows the case, and set a small word budget for the overview.

difficulties.pattern: Describing a framework or theory at length without applying it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that define a model or list its components with little reference to the case.
difficulties.response: Require every analytical paragraph to contain case evidence and an implication for the issue.

difficulties.pattern: Recommendations not linked to the analysis, or not feasible.
difficulties.revealedBy: New ideas appearing for the first time in the recommendations.
difficulties.response: Have learners trace each recommendation back to an issue and forward to feasibility and risk.

diagnostic.task: Give a mini-case and ask for the most important issue and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a prioritised issue with supporting case evidence and an implication.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names an issue without justification.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Retells the case.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: business and other pathways introduce short cases with guided frameworks. In-sessional undergraduate: discipline-specific case studies in business, health, law, education and engineering, ideally co-taught with subject staff. Taught postgraduate: professional master's programmes rely heavily on case analysis, often with complex cases and group work.

guidance.summary: Nathan (2013) shows that business school case report writing is problem-oriented and recommendation-driven and argues for making its structure and expectations explicit to students. Bhatia (1993) offers a framework for analysing professional genres through the communicative purposes of their users, which suits reports written for simulated clients and managers, and Gardner and Nesi (2013) note the professional-practice purpose of such genres. Teach the findings–conclusions–recommendations chain, the role of the executive summary and analytical use of frameworks, and check local templates because business schools differ.

activities.title: Findings, conclusions, recommendations
learnerActions: Given a set of findings, write a conclusion for each
Derive a recommendation from each conclusion
Prioritise the recommendations by impact and feasibility
Check that no recommendation lacks a supporting finding
activities.intendedInsight: Recommendations persuade when they can be traced back to findings.
activities.rationale: Reflects the recommendation-driven structure of business case genres (Nathan, 2013).

activities.title: Writing for a busy manager
learnerActions: Read two versions of a report introduction, one front-loaded and one background-heavy
Decide which better supports a decision and why
Rewrite a background-heavy section so that the key message comes first
activities.intendedInsight: Professional readers prioritise purpose, conclusions and actions.
activities.rationale: Communicative purpose shapes the structure of professional genres (Bhatia, 1993).

difficulties.pattern: Essay-like discussion with vague or missing recommendations.
difficulties.revealedBy: A final section that summarises rather than recommends.
difficulties.response: Use the findings–conclusions–recommendations chain and require a recommendations section mapped to the conclusions.

difficulties.pattern: Management frameworks used as checklists.
difficulties.revealedBy: Bulleted framework lists with no prioritisation or implications.
difficulties.response: Require learners to prioritise framework items and state the implication of each for the problem.

difficulties.pattern: Bullet points used for analysis, or avoided where they would help.
difficulties.revealedBy: Analysis fragmented into bullets, or long recommendations buried in prose.
difficulties.response: Use bullets for parallel items such as recommendations and continuous prose for analysis and justification, following the brief.

diagnostic.task: Ask: what is the difference between a conclusion and a recommendation in a business report?
diagnostic.strongResponse: A conclusion is a judgement drawn from findings; a recommendation proposes an action that follows from a conclusion.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a vague or partly correct distinction.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats them as the same.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: simple reports in business pathways. Pre-sessional: business-specific pre-sessionals may use report assessments. In-sessional undergraduate: business, management and accounting reports. Taught postgraduate: MBA and management master's reports, often for simulated clients and with group authorship.

guidance.summary: Gardner and Nesi (2013) identify Design Specification as a genre family that prepares students for professional practice, particularly in engineering. Trimble's (1985) rhetorical approach to scientific and technical English highlights the description, definition, classification and visual–verbal relationships on which technical reports depend. Prioritise justification of decisions against requirements and integration of visuals, and consult departmental templates, professional-body expectations and module briefs, because formats differ between engineering branches, computing and product design.

activities.title: Requirements to criteria
learnerActions: Extract requirements and constraints from a design brief
Rewrite vague requirements as measurable ones
Use them as criteria in a decision matrix for two options
Write a selection paragraph that refers to the matrix
activities.intendedInsight: Design decisions are justified by explicit, measurable criteria.
activities.rationale: Supports the justificatory purpose of the Design Specification family (Gardner & Nesi, 2013).

activities.title: Text and diagram together
learnerActions: Describe a component using a labelled diagram
Write a paragraph that refers to the diagram and explains each part's function
Ask a partner to identify the parts from your text alone
activities.intendedInsight: Technical description depends on precise integration of text and visuals.
activities.rationale: Trimble (1985) treats visual–verbal relationships as a core rhetorical feature of technical writing.

difficulties.pattern: Narrating what the team did chronologically instead of justifying decisions.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'First we ..., then we ...' structures with little evaluation.
difficulties.response: Restructure sections around decisions, options and criteria, keeping chronology for logs or appendices.

difficulties.pattern: Imprecise requirements and evaluations ('the design is efficient and good').
difficulties.revealedBy: Unmeasurable claims without values or units.
difficulties.response: Require quantification with units and tolerances, and link each evaluative claim to a requirement.

diagnostic.task: Ask learners to justify, in three sentences, choosing one of two familiar products for a stated purpose.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names explicit criteria, compares the options on them with values where possible, and acknowledges a trade-off.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives criteria but no comparison, or comparison without criteria.
diagnostic.gapResponse: States a preference without reasons.

guidance.contextNotes: In-sessional undergraduate: engineering, computing and design programmes, best embedded in project modules with subject staff. Taught postgraduate: MSc engineering and computing projects, where professional standards and group-authored reports are common.

guidance.summary: Gardner and Nesi (2013) include proposals among genres preparing students for professional and research practice. Creswell and Creswell (2018) provide widely used proposal structures for quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods studies that emphasise alignment between purpose, questions and methods, and Paltridge and Starfield (2020) discuss the proposal as a persuasive text addressed to supervisors and committees. Connor and Mauranen's (1999) move analysis of research grant proposals identifies persuasive moves (such as territory, gap, goal, means and benefits) that can be adapted to student proposals, which are far less competitive. Departmental templates differ substantially and must guide the structure.

activities.title: Proposal skeleton from the template
learnerActions: Collect your department's proposal template and assessment criteria
Write one sentence for each section
Check alignment: does each question have a method and a data source?
Ask a peer to review feasibility within the time available
activities.intendedInsight: A convincing proposal is aligned, feasible and shaped by the local template.
activities.rationale: Applies the alignment of purpose, questions and methods emphasised by Creswell and Creswell (2018).

activities.title: Persuasive moves
learnerActions: Label the moves in a model proposal rationale (territory, gap, aim, method, benefit)
Identify the language that persuades the reader of significance and feasibility
Draft your own rationale paragraph using the moves
activities.intendedInsight: A proposal is an argument for the project, not a description of it.
activities.rationale: Adapts Connor and Mauranen's (1999) analysis of grant proposal moves to student proposals.

difficulties.pattern: Over-ambitious scope for the time and resources available.
difficulties.revealedBy: Multiple broad questions, large samples or several methods in a short project.
difficulties.response: Narrow the questions and test feasibility against the timeline and access, with supervisor input.

difficulties.pattern: A rationale based only on personal interest ('I have always been interested in ...').
difficulties.revealedBy: Significance argued from the writer's biography rather than from literature or need.
difficulties.response: Allow a brief note of motivation where the brief permits, but require significance to be argued from the literature, a gap or a practical need.

difficulties.pattern: Ethics treated as a formality.
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic statements ('there are no ethical issues') for projects involving people or data.
difficulties.response: Discuss consent, confidentiality, data management and risk for the specific project and link to the institution's ethics process.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to state their project aim, one research question and the data that will answer it in three sentences.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A focused aim, an answerable question and feasible, aligned data.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A focused aim but a misaligned or unfeasible data source.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A topic rather than an aim or question.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional: short proposals for extended projects, closely supervised. In-sessional undergraduate: final-year project and dissertation proposals. Taught postgraduate: dissertation proposals are frequently assessed and are followed by ethics applications, often within weeks.

guidance.summary: Executive summaries are professional rather than research genres: Bhatia (1993) argues that professional genres are best understood through the communicative purposes of their users, here a reader deciding whether and how to act. They share with abstracts the demand for a stand-alone condensation of a longer text (Swales & Feak, 2009) but prioritise findings and recommendations over method. Teach by comparing an abstract, an introduction and an executive summary for the same report, and have learners write for a named reader facing a specific decision.

activities.title: Three openings compared
learnerActions: Read an abstract, an introduction and an executive summary written for the same report
List what each includes and omits and in what order
Identify the reader and purpose of each
Write a rule of thumb for each text type in one sentence
activities.intendedInsight: Different reader purposes produce different selections and orderings of the same content.
activities.rationale: Comparison by purpose follows Bhatia's (1993) approach to professional genres; the abstract provides a familiar point of contrast (Swales & Feak, 2009).

activities.title: Two sentences first
learnerActions: State the report's main finding and main recommendation in two sentences
Test them on a partner who has not read the report: could they act on them?
Expand to the required length, adding supporting findings in order of importance
Check that nothing appears that is not in the report
activities.intendedInsight: The executive summary is built outward from the key message rather than compiled section by section.
activities.rationale: Front-loading serves the decision-making reader that defines the genre's purpose (Bhatia, 1993).

difficulties.pattern: The summary is written as an introduction, describing background and what the report will do.
difficulties.revealedBy: Phrases such as 'This report will examine ...' and no findings or recommendations.
difficulties.response: Contrast introduction and executive summary directly, and require findings and recommendations in the first paragraph.

difficulties.pattern: One sentence copied or paraphrased from each section in report order.
difficulties.revealedBy: A summary that mirrors the report's table of contents and gives method as much space as findings.
difficulties.response: Have learners rank content by importance to the reader before drafting, and allow the order to depart from the report's.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain, in two or three sentences, how an executive summary differs from an abstract.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Notes the decision-making reader, the emphasis on findings and recommendations over method, and stand-alone use.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Says it is 'a longer abstract' or notes only position in the document.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats it as an introduction.

guidance.contextNotes: In-sessional undergraduate: business, engineering and some social science reports require executive summaries, often as a separately marked element. Taught postgraduate: management, public policy and public health programmes use them routinely, and they recur in professional practice.
reviewNotes: No item in the closed bibliography analyses executive summaries directly; the citations support only the general claims about professional genres and abstracts.

guidance.summary: Treat the policy brief as a professional genre whose structure follows its users' purposes (Bhatia, 1993): busy readers need key messages first, a clear problem, a fair account of evidence and actionable options. A recurrent challenge is presenting evidence accessibly without distortion; Gigerenzer et al. (2007) show that statistical information is better understood when presented as absolute risks and natural frequencies rather than relative risks alone, which is directly relevant to briefs on health, education or social policy. Analyse briefs from the organisations learners might write for, as templates and expectations vary.

activities.title: Key messages from research
learnerActions: Read the abstract and findings of a policy-relevant study
Draft three key messages for a named policy reader
Check each against the evidence for overstatement
Rewrite any statistics as absolute figures or natural frequencies where helpful
activities.intendedInsight: Policy messages must be both actionable and faithful to the strength of the evidence.
activities.rationale: Applies Gigerenzer et al.'s (2007) principles for transparent risk communication to the genre's central move.

activities.title: Brief anatomy
learnerActions: Compare two published policy briefs from different organisations
Label their sections and identify how evidence and recommendations are presented
Note how visuals and headings serve a skimming reader
Draft a template for a brief in your field
activities.intendedInsight: Policy briefs share a purpose-driven logic but differ in template by organisation.
activities.rationale: Analysing professional genres through their purposes and users follows Bhatia (1993).

difficulties.pattern: Writing an academic literature review with recommendations added at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long background, dense citation and recommendations only in the final paragraph.
difficulties.response: Insist on key messages first and a strict page limit; move citations to endnotes or links where the template allows.

difficulties.pattern: Overstating certainty or causal effects to make recommendations persuasive.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unqualified claims ('X will reduce Y') from observational or limited evidence.
difficulties.response: Teach plain-language ways of signalling evidence strength ('strong evidence suggests', 'early findings indicate') and check each message against its source.

difficulties.pattern: Recommendations that are vague or addressed to no one ('More should be done').
difficulties.revealedBy: Recommendations without an actor, action or time frame.
difficulties.response: Require each recommendation to name who should do what, by when, and at roughly what cost or risk.

diagnostic.task: Give learners a research finding and ask for one recommendation for a named policy actor.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A specific, feasible action for a named actor, worded within the strength of the evidence.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A specific action that overstates the evidence, or a cautious but vague action.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A general statement with no actor or action.

guidance.contextNotes: In-sessional undergraduate: occasional assessments in politics, development, public health and environmental studies. Taught postgraduate: common in public policy, international development, public health and education master's programmes. PGR: briefs are a route to research impact and engagement, often written with institutional policy or knowledge-exchange teams.
reviewNotes: The closed bibliography contains no genre analysis of policy briefs; adding a verified source on policy-brief writing would strengthen this topic. Overlaps with dss.policy-analysis.

guidance.summary: Portfolios operationalise Schön's (1983) idea of the reflective practitioner in assessed form, typically combining logs, reflective accounts and evidence mapped to competencies. Moon (2004) shows that reflective writing ranges from description to deeper, critical reflection, and Ryan (2011) argues that the language of reflection must be taught explicitly; both apply to the reflective components of portfolios. The less-discussed demands are documentary: concise factual logging, selection and annotation of evidence against standards, and confidentiality. Work from the specific professional standards and templates learners must use, ideally with placement tutors.

activities.title: Evidence to competency
learnerActions: Take one competency statement from your professional standards
Collect three possible pieces of evidence from your practice
Rank them by how directly they demonstrate the competency
Write an annotation for the best one explaining what it shows and what it does not
activities.intendedInsight: Evidence must be selected and explicitly argued to meet a standard; inclusion alone does not demonstrate competence.
activities.rationale: Connects reflective practice (Schön, 1983) to the argumentative work of evidencing competence.

activities.title: From log entry to reflective account
learnerActions: Read a factual log entry about a placement incident
Identify what in it is worth reflecting on and why
Write a short reflective account using the language of reasoning and reconstruction
Link it to one theory or standard
activities.intendedInsight: Logs record; reflective accounts interpret and plan, and each has its own language.
activities.rationale: Applies Ryan's (2011) reflective language resources and Moon's (2004) levels of reflection to portfolio components.

difficulties.pattern: Including everything rather than selecting and annotating evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Large portfolios with unannotated certificates, notes and documents.
difficulties.response: Limit evidence per competency and require an annotation for every item.

difficulties.pattern: Breaching confidentiality through identifiable details about patients, pupils, clients or colleagues.
difficulties.revealedBy: Names, locations or distinctive details in logs and reflections.
difficulties.response: Teach anonymisation conventions of the relevant profession and review drafts before submission.

difficulties.pattern: Reflection reduced to descriptive logging.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accounts that list activities without interpretation or learning.
difficulties.response: Return to reflective writing models and require an explicit link to theory or a standard in each account.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to annotate one piece of evidence against a given competency in 80–100 words.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explicitly maps the evidence to the competency, specifies what it demonstrates and notes its limits.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes the evidence without explicit mapping.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the competency or the evidence title.

guidance.contextNotes: In-sessional undergraduate: nursing, midwifery, allied health, teacher education, social work and engineering placements, where professional bodies define standards. Taught postgraduate: professional master's and conversion programmes, often with e-portfolio platforms and tight placement schedules.

guidance.summary: Public-facing writing intensifies the engagement resources Hyland (2005) describes for academic discourse, and Hyland (2010, proposed reference) compares how popular and professional science texts construct proximity to their readers differently, which gives learners a principled basis for adapting their writing. Mewburn and Thomson (2013, proposed reference) analysed academic blogs and found a range of audiences and purposes, so 'blog' is not a single genre. Teach learners to adapt their own academic texts for a named public, to keep fidelity to the evidence, and to consider their public academic identity.

activities.title: Same finding, two readers
learnerActions: Compare a research article's abstract with a blog post or news piece on the same study
List changes in structure, voice, engagement and treatment of uncertainty
Identify any place where the public version distorts or overstates the finding
Rewrite one paragraph of your own assignment for a public reader
activities.intendedInsight: Adapting for the public changes structure and voice but should not change what the evidence shows.
activities.rationale: Draws on Hyland's (2010, proposed) comparison of popular and professional science and on Hyland's (2005) account of engagement resources.

activities.title: Purpose and platform
learnerActions: Read three academic blog posts with different purposes (explaining research, commenting on policy, reflecting on academic life)
Identify each post's likely audience and how it addresses them
Plan a post for one purpose and audience relevant to your field
activities.intendedInsight: Academic blogs serve varied purposes and audiences, and these shape their style.
activities.rationale: Reflects Mewburn and Thomson's (2013, proposed) finding that academic blogs vary in audience and purpose.

difficulties.pattern: Writing a shortened academic paper, dense with terminology and citations.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unexplained jargon, formal citations and a slow build-up to the main point.
difficulties.response: Have learners state the main point in one plain sentence first, then test drafts on a non-specialist reader.

difficulties.pattern: Overcorrecting into hype or oversimplification.
difficulties.revealedBy: Claims such as 'scientists prove' or 'breakthrough' for tentative findings.
difficulties.response: Practise plain-language signals of uncertainty and compare drafts with the source's own claims.

difficulties.pattern: Anxiety about public visibility or criticism online.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to publish, or extreme hedging and impersonality in public drafts.
difficulties.response: Discuss platform choice, moderation and institutional support; start with internal or departmental outlets.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain a key finding from their field to a non-specialist in three sentences in writing.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate, jargon-free, leads with significance and signals uncertainty appropriately.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate but jargon-heavy, or accessible but overstated.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Inaccurate or incomprehensible to a lay reader.

guidance.contextNotes: In-sessional undergraduate: blog and opinion-piece assessments are increasingly common in media, politics and science communication modules. Taught postgraduate: public-facing assessments in policy, development and communication programmes. PGR: blogs and outreach writing as part of research engagement and impact, often supported by institutional communications teams.
reviewNotes: Two of the three citations are proposed references; if they cannot be verified, remove the related claims and rely on hyland2005stance and the reg.non-specialist-audiences prerequisite. Overlaps with pub.research-engagement.
