guidance.summary: Paltridge (2002) identified several macrostructures for theses and dissertations (traditional simple, traditional complex, topic-based and compilation) and showed that published advice under-represents this variety; Paltridge and Starfield (2020) offer practical guidance for second-language writers and their supervisors. Research on master's dissertations shows where high- and low-rated work differ, for example in the range of rhetorical functions of citation (Petrić, 2007), and Hopkins and Dudley-Evans (1988) analysed the moves of discussion sections in MSc dissertations. Use departmental handbooks and past dissertations as primary sources, and present the dissertation as one argument developed across chapters.

activities.title: Past dissertation analysis
learnerActions: With departmental permission, examine two high-graded dissertations from your programme
Map each chapter's function and its share of the total word count
Compare the maps with the handbook's guidance and with each other
Draft your own chapter plan with functions and word allocations
activities.intendedInsight: Dissertation structures vary within a department; functions and proportions matter more than chapter names.
activities.rationale: Paltridge (2002) shows that actual practice is more varied than published advice suggests, so local examples are essential.

activities.title: What citation is doing
learnerActions: Classify the citations in two pages of a dissertation by function (attribution, support, comparison, evaluation, establishing links)
Compare the distribution with a page of your own draft
Revise one paragraph to use citation for comparison or evaluation rather than attribution alone
activities.intendedInsight: Higher-rated work uses citation to do more rhetorical work than attribution.
activities.rationale: Based on Petrić's (2007) comparison of citation functions in high- and low-rated master's theses.

difficulties.pattern: Treating the dissertation as a long essay or as a set of separate assignments.
difficulties.revealedBy: Chapters that do not refer to each other; research questions that disappear after the introduction.
difficulties.response: Have learners write chapter introductions and conclusions that state each chapter's contribution to answering the questions.

difficulties.pattern: A thin discussion that restates findings without interpreting them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussion chapters that repeat results and add little reference to literature.
difficulties.response: Analyse discussion moves in local exemplars and require each finding to be interpreted against the literature.

difficulties.pattern: A literature review disconnected from the study.
difficulties.revealedBy: A broad review that does not lead to the research questions or return in the discussion.
difficulties.response: Require the review's final section to justify the research questions and the discussion to revisit the review's key themes.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe, in five bullet points, what each chapter of their planned dissertation will do.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Functional descriptions linked to the research questions, with a coherent through-line.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate chapter names with topical rather than functional descriptions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot outline a structure or lists generic headings.

guidance.contextNotes: In-sessional undergraduate: final-year dissertations and projects, whose length, format and empirical expectations vary greatly between disciplines. Taught postgraduate: the dissertation is often written over a compressed summer period, carries heavy credit weighting and may be the learner's first extended research text, so early planning support is especially valuable.

guidance.summary: Swales and Feak (2009) treat abstracts as a genre with recognisable moves and linguistic choices, and Santos (1996) proposed a five-move model for research article abstracts in applied linguistics (situating the research, presenting it, describing the methodology, summarising results and discussing the research). Student abstracts adapt these moves to assessment purposes: the marker uses the abstract to check that the student can represent their work accurately and concisely. Analyse local exemplars, because poster, dissertation and report abstracts differ in length and format, and some fields require structured abstracts.

activities.title: Move check
learnerActions: Label the moves in three abstracts from your department or field
Note the tense and voice used in each move
Check your own draft abstract for missing or over-long moves
Revise to the word limit
activities.intendedInsight: Abstracts have predictable moves with typical tense patterns, and completeness matters within tight limits.
activities.rationale: Applies the move models of Santos (1996) and Swales and Feak (2009) as a revision checklist.

activities.title: From indicative to informative
learnerActions: Read an abstract that says what the report 'will discuss' without stating results
Rewrite it to state the actual findings and conclusion
Compare which version would better serve a marker or a reader deciding whether to read on
activities.intendedInsight: Informative abstracts state findings; indicative ones only describe topics.
activities.rationale: The distinction between informative and indicative abstracts is a standard element of abstract instruction (Swales & Feak, 2009).

difficulties.pattern: Abstract written as an introduction or table of contents.
difficulties.revealedBy: Background-heavy abstracts that preview sections and omit findings.
difficulties.response: Require one sentence each for method, findings and conclusion before adding context.

difficulties.pattern: Inconsistent or unmotivated tense shifts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Methods in the present and conclusions in the past, or random alternation.
difficulties.response: Show the typical tense pattern by move and the reasons for it, noting that local conventions differ.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a 100-word abstract of a project or assignment they have completed.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All core moves, specific findings and appropriate tenses within the limit.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Most moves present but findings vague or method missing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: An introduction or topic description without findings.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional: abstracts for extended projects and posters. In-sessional undergraduate: abstracts for final-year projects, lab reports and posters. Taught postgraduate: dissertation abstracts, sometimes structured, and abstracts for student conferences.

authorNotes: ess.essay-types (Essay Construction) overlaps substantially with the GES essay genres (argumentative, discussion, compare-and-contrast, explanation, problem–solution). Suggest scoping ess.essay-types as a brief conceptual overview that these genre topics may take as a soft prerequisite, or retiring it in favour of ges.genre-families.

ges.genre-concept overlaps with acu.discourse-communities. I have not linked them to avoid a potential cross-strand cycle; whichever strand links them should choose one direction (suggested: acu.discourse-communities as a soft prerequisite of ges.genre-concept).
ges.exam-essay overlaps with exm.timed-writing; the latter should remain the generic procedure and the former the genre, which is how they are linked here.

ges.literature-review-assignment and res.literature-review are appropriately split (coursework versus research writing); the research strand already links res.literature-review to this topic, which is the right direction.

ges.reflective-writing overlaps with dhl.reflective-practice and lrn.reflective-logs; dhl.reflective-practice already takes it as a prerequisite. lrn.reflective-logs is not linked to reflective writing to avoid presuming the learning strand's direction.
ges.summary-response is largely a North American composition genre; in UK contexts it is mainly an EAP or foundation teaching genre. Consider noting this in the skeleton scope.

The compare-and-contrast, explanation and problem–solution essays are partly 'cognitive genres' (in Bruce's sense) rather than distinct social genres; they are valid EAP teaching genres but departments rarely name them. A future revision could fold them into one topic on essay rhetorical patterns.

grp.case-study overlaps with dbe.business-case-analysis and dhl.case-reports-care-plans. The disciplinary strand already takes grp.case-study as a prerequisite of both, which is the right direction; this topic covers the cross-disciplinary genre.
grp.business-report overlaps with dbe.professional-genres, which already takes it as a prerequisite.
grp.technical-design-report overlaps with dad.design-rationale, dse.protocols-specifications and dse.software-documentation; suggest those topics take it as a soft prerequisite where appropriate.
grp.project-proposal overlaps with res.research-proposal (doctoral and grant proposals); suggest res.research-proposal take grp.project-proposal as a soft prerequisite.

grp.policy-brief overlaps with dss.policy-analysis; one should be scoped as the short advocacy genre (this topic) and the other as the analytical process, and linked dss.policy-analysis -> grp.policy-brief or left unlinked.

grp.public-writing overlaps heavily with pub.research-engagement and reg.non-specialist-audiences. Suggest pub.research-engagement be scoped as strategy and channels (impact, social media planning) and this topic as the writing of specific public genres, with pub.research-engagement taking it as a soft prerequisite.
grp.student-abstract overlaps with res.abstracts and grp.executive-summary; suggest res.abstracts take grp.student-abstract as a soft prerequisite.
grp.dissertation-overview overlaps with res.thesis-macrostructure (doctoral); suggest that topic take this one as a soft prerequisite.
grp.professional-portfolio overlaps with dhl.reflective-practice and mmd.digital-assessments (e-portfolios). It is not linked to either, to avoid presuming those strands' directions.

grp.dissertation-overview is typed GENRE in the skeleton but its scope note ('structure, scope and expectations') is partly conceptual; it is written here as a genre with planning-oriented mastery evidence.

Gap: the Empathy Writing family identified by Gardner and Nesi (2013) (writing in role for a lay or professional reader, such as a client letter, patient leaflet or information sheet) has no dedicated topic; grp.public-writing, grp.policy-brief and res.ethics-documentation cover it only partially.
